Longitudinal and Survival Analysis of a Simulated Clinical Study

Tanvir Ahmed

1 Introduction

This project was my final assignment for a university course in Longitudinal and Survival Data Analysis. The dataset is simulated; my course instructor provided it.

The study has 240 patients with a chronic disease. Each patient received either the standard treatment (treatment = 0) or a new treatment (treatment = 1).

  • A biomarker was measured four times: at the start (month 0) and at 3, 6 and 12 months.
  • Patients were then followed for up to seven years to see whether they died.

I answer two questions:

  1. Does the biomarker change over time, and does the change differ between the two treatments?
  2. Do patients on the new treatment live longer?
library(tidyverse)  # reading, reshaping and plotting data
library(lme4)       # linear mixed model
library(lmerTest)   # p-values for the mixed model
library(survival)   # Kaplan-Meier, log-rank test and Cox model

2 Data

data_wide <- read.table("data/extra_data.txt", header = TRUE)
head(data_wide)
##   id treatment age sex    bio_0    bio_3    bio_6   bio_12    follow death
## 1  1         1  77   1 70.30169 55.00377 58.34121 43.48814 2.6428327     0
## 2  2         1  79   0 64.88370 60.05012 61.05127 51.59900 2.4254194     0
## 3  3         0  64   0 68.23759 59.34814 58.49068 55.68577 0.1173484     1
## 4  4         0  69   1 64.75539 60.23102 55.73027 48.05589 0.1770661     0
## 5  5         1  48   0 69.14116 58.95023 60.16525 47.09809 1.3736019     0

Variable Meaning
id patient number
treatment 0 = standard, 1 = new
age age in years
sex 0 = female, 1 = male
bio_0, bio_3, bio_6, bio_12 biomarker at month 0, 3, 6 and 12
follow follow-up time in years
death 1 = died, 0 = still alive at the end of follow-up (censored)

The data have one row per patient. For the longitudinal model I need one row per measurement, so I reshape the data from wide to long format.

data_long <- data_wide |>
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("bio_"),
               names_to = "visit", values_to = "biomarker") |>
  mutate(month = as.numeric(sub("bio_", "", visit)),
         group = factor(treatment, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("Standard", "New")))

head(data_long)

nrow(data_long)   # 240 patients x 4 visits = 960 rows

3 Part 1: How does the biomarker change over time?

3.1 Plot

Each thin line is one patient. The thick lines are the average of each group.

group_means <- data_long |>
  group_by(group, month) |>
  summarise(biomarker = mean(biomarker))

ggplot(data_long, aes(x = month, y = biomarker, colour = group)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = id), alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_line(data = group_means, linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_point(data = group_means, size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 3, 6, 12)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Standard" = "#2C7FB8", "New" = "#D95F0E")) +
  labs(x = "Month", y = "Biomarker", colour = "Treatment",
       title = "Biomarker over 12 months") +
  theme_minimal()

group_means |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = month, values_from = biomarker, names_prefix = "Month ") |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
group Month 0 Month 3 Month 6 Month 12
Standard 64.6 62.5 59.4 54.0
New 61.6 56.7 51.6 44.1

The biomarker goes down in both groups, and it goes down faster in the new-treatment group. The plot also shows that some patients are always high and others always low, so measurements from the same patient are related.

3.2 Linear mixed model

A normal regression assumes every row is independent. Here each patient has four measurements, so they are not independent. A linear mixed model with a random intercept handles this by giving each patient their own starting level.

The model is:

biomarker = time + treatment + time × treatment + (a random starting level for each patient)

The time × treatment term tests whether the biomarker changes at a different speed in the two groups.

model <- lmer(biomarker ~ month * treatment + (1 | id), data = data_long)
summary(model)
## Linear mixed model fit by REML. t-tests use Satterthwaite's method [
## lmerModLmerTest]
## Formula: biomarker ~ month * treatment + (1 | id)
##    Data: data_long
## 
## REML criterion at convergence: 5576.4
## 
## Scaled residuals: 
##      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
## -2.87253 -0.59480 -0.00796  0.59056  2.87380 
## 
## Random effects:
##  Groups   Name        Variance Std.Dev.
##  id       (Intercept) 17.08    4.133   
##  Residual             12.07    3.475   
## Number of obs: 960, groups:  id, 240
## 
## Fixed effects:
##                  Estimate Std. Error        df t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)      64.82788    0.42609 343.55466 152.147  < 2e-16 ***
## month            -0.89848    0.03383 718.00000 -26.562  < 2e-16 ***
## treatment        -3.69341    0.64114 343.55466  -5.761 1.86e-08 ***
## month:treatment  -0.55811    0.05090 718.00000 -10.965  < 2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Correlation of Fixed Effects:
##             (Intr) month  trtmnt
## month       -0.417              
## treatment   -0.665  0.277       
## mnth:trtmnt  0.277 -0.665 -0.417
confint(model, parm = "beta_", method = "Wald")
##                      2.5 %     97.5 %
## (Intercept)     63.9927582 65.6629937
## month           -0.9647815 -0.8321854
## treatment       -4.9500154 -2.4367960
## month:treatment -0.6578665 -0.4583477

What the results mean

  • month (about −0.90): with the standard treatment, the biomarker goes down by about 0.9 units every month.
  • month:treatment (about −0.56, p < 0.001): with the new treatment, it goes down about 0.56 units faster per month, so about 1.46 units per month in total. After 12 months that is roughly 6.7 units more decrease than with the standard treatment.
  • treatment (about −3.7): the new-treatment group already started about 3.7 units lower at month 0. This is a difference between the groups at the start, not an effect of the treatment.
  • Random effects: the variance between patients (id) is larger than the leftover variance (Residual). Most of the variation comes from patients being different from each other, which is why a mixed model is needed.

4 Part 2: Do patients on the new treatment live longer?

4.1 Kaplan–Meier curves

The Kaplan–Meier method estimates the probability of still being alive at each point in time. It also handles patients who were still alive at the end of follow-up (censored).

km <- survfit(Surv(follow, death) ~ treatment, data = data_wide)
km
## Call: survfit(formula = Surv(follow, death) ~ treatment, data = data_wide)
## 
##               n events median 0.95LCL 0.95UCL
## treatment=0 134     60   3.46    2.93      NA
## treatment=1 106     31     NA    4.55      NA
plot(km, col = c("#2C7FB8", "#D95F0E"), lwd = 2, mark.time = TRUE,
     xlab = "Years", ylab = "Probability of survival",
     main = "Kaplan–Meier survival curves")
legend("bottomleft", legend = c("Standard", "New"),
       col = c("#2C7FB8", "#D95F0E"), lwd = 2)

summary(km, times = 3)
## Call: survfit(formula = Surv(follow, death) ~ treatment, data = data_wide)
## 
##                 treatment=0 
##         time       n.risk      n.event     survival      std.err lower 95% CI 
##       3.0000      40.0000      49.0000       0.5730       0.0486       0.4852 
## upper 95% CI 
##       0.6767 
## 
##                 treatment=1 
##         time       n.risk      n.event     survival      std.err lower 95% CI 
##       3.0000      39.0000      24.0000       0.7301       0.0484       0.6411 
## upper 95% CI 
##       0.8314

The new-treatment curve stays above the standard curve during the whole follow-up. After 3 years about 73% of the new-treatment patients are still alive, compared with about 57% of the standard-treatment patients.

4.2 Log-rank test

The log-rank test checks whether the two survival curves are statistically different.

survdiff(Surv(follow, death) ~ treatment, data = data_wide)
## Call:
## survdiff(formula = Surv(follow, death) ~ treatment, data = data_wide)
## 
##               N Observed Expected (O-E)^2/E (O-E)^2/V
## treatment=0 134       60     47.6      3.23       6.8
## treatment=1 106       31     43.4      3.54       6.8
## 
##  Chisq= 6.8  on 1 degrees of freedom, p= 0.009

The p-value is 0.009, which is below 0.05. The survival curves of the two groups are significantly different.

4.3 Cox proportional hazards model

The log-rank test does not adjust for other variables. The Cox model estimates the effect of treatment while taking age and sex into account. The result is a hazard ratio (HR):

  • HR < 1: lower risk of death
  • HR = 1: no difference
  • HR > 1: higher risk of death
cox <- coxph(Surv(follow, death) ~ treatment + age + sex, data = data_wide)
summary(cox)
## Call:
## coxph(formula = Surv(follow, death) ~ treatment + age + sex, 
##     data = data_wide)
## 
##   n= 240, number of events= 91 
## 
##               coef exp(coef) se(coef)      z Pr(>|z|)   
## treatment -0.57768   0.56120  0.22345 -2.585  0.00973 **
## age        0.03195   1.03246  0.01530  2.088  0.03678 * 
## sex        0.12285   1.13072  0.21203  0.579  0.56231   
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
##           exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95
## treatment    0.5612     1.7819    0.3622    0.8696
## age          1.0325     0.9686    1.0020    1.0639
## sex          1.1307     0.8844    0.7462    1.7133
## 
## Concordance= 0.617  (se = 0.029 )
## Likelihood ratio test= 11.93  on 3 df,   p=0.008
## Wald test            = 11.3  on 3 df,   p=0.01
## Score (logrank) test = 11.47  on 3 df,   p=0.009

What the results mean

  • Treatment: HR = 0.56 (95% CI 0.36 to 0.87, p = 0.01). Patients on the new treatment have about 44% lower risk of death than patients on the standard treatment of the same age and sex.
  • Age: HR = 1.03. Each extra year of age increases the risk of death by about 3%.
  • Sex: HR = 1.13, p = 0.6. There is no clear difference between men and women.

4.3.1 Checking the proportional hazards assumption

The Cox model assumes that the hazard ratio stays the same over time. The cox.zph() function tests this. A p-value above 0.05 means the assumption is OK.

cox.zph(cox)
##            chisq df    p
## treatment 0.0719  1 0.79
## age       0.8605  1 0.35
## sex       0.7530  1 0.39
## GLOBAL    1.5502  3 0.67

All p-values are above 0.05, so the assumption holds.

5 Conclusions

  1. Biomarker: the biomarker decreases over time in both groups, and it decreases faster with the new treatment (about 1.46 vs 0.90 units per month).
  2. Survival: patients on the new treatment live longer. The Kaplan–Meier curves and the log-rank test (p = 0.009) show a clear difference.
  3. Cox model: after adjusting for age and sex, the new treatment lowers the risk of death by about 44% (HR 0.56).

Limitation: the data are simulated, so the results only show how these methods work. They say nothing about a real treatment.
